Chapter 8: The Science of Forgotten Knowledge
Picture the traveler now stepping into the world of science—a place where questions are endless, and doubt is almost a badge of honor. But here's the thing: once you see the evidence, you just can't unsee it.
In a cramped, cluttered university office, a geologist welcomes the traveler and gently sets down a handful of rock samples—taken from the very base of the Sphinx. The geologist points out the unusual erosion patterns. They're not what you'd expect in the dry, dusty air of modern Egypt. Instead, these marks tell a story of heavy, pounding rain.
But when did that happen? The last time such downpours soaked the Giza plateau was over ten thousand years ago. Suddenly, a chill runs through the traveler. If the geologist is right, the Sphinx could have been carved at the end of the last Ice Age—long before the pharaohs even dreamed of building pyramids.
The journey continues to a laboratory, where a physicist demonstrates something fascinating: the precession of the Earth. Imagine the planet slowly wobbling over thousands of years, shifting the positions of the stars in the night sky. The physicist shows how ancient monuments align perfectly—not with the sky we see today, but with the sky as it appeared ages ago. The traveler can’t help but marvel at the precision. Someone, way back when, understood the cosmos with a depth that matches our own modern science.
And then, in South America, the traveler meets an engineer obsessed with the mystery of the megalithic walls—massive stones fitted together so tightly, you couldn’t slide a piece of paper between them. There’s no mortar, no cement—just pure ingenuity. The engineer wonders aloud: did the builders use some lost technology? Maybe sound, or heat, or even special chemicals to shape and move these giants? It sounds wild, but the traveler remembers legends from around the world—stories of magic songs that could move mountains.
All these encounters leave the traveler deep in thought. Why do so many scientists hesitate to explore these mysteries? The traveler understands—after all, science thrives on skepticism. But there’s also a risk in ignoring evidence just because it doesn’t fit the usual story. The traveler feels a growing urgency. If we don’t keep asking, if we stop searching, the real story—the truth—could slip away forever.
